title: Powerlifting Performance Explorer
text:
This site uses public powerlifting meet data instead of a static training plan. The dataset contains tens of thousands of lifter records and includes bodyweight, sex, age, and the best squat, bench, deadlift, and total for each athlete. That gives a real foundation for asking questions like: which bodyweight ranges support the strongest totals, and which lifts respond most strongly to size and bodyweight?

Public meet files do not consistently report height, so the most reliable body-size signal in the dataset is bodyweight and weight class. The analysis therefore focuses on bodyweight, age, and performance rather than a height-only model.



                            
                                            





The sample includes more than 50,000 lifter observations
Bodyweight is strongly associated with total lift output
Men and women show different performance curves, but the trend remains: larger bodyweight ranges tend to support larger totals
This is a real observational data set, not a generic plan or static recommendation

The homepage is therefore built around actual meet data and the question: which bodyweight ranges pair best with strong squat, bench, and deadlift performance?

title: Exploration
text:
The most useful training question in the data is not simply “who lifts the most?” It is: how does bodyweight relate to max squat, bench, and deadlift performance, and which bodyweight ranges tend to pair best with each lift?




                            
                                            


The pattern is strong: total lift output rises with bodyweight in both sexes, but the relationship is clearly not one-size-fits-all. There are broad bands where lifters are unusually productive for their bodyweight, which suggests that weight class and individual structure matter.





                            
                                            


This view makes the training story more concrete. Squat and deadlift usually continue climbing as bodyweight rises, while bench performance has a slightly different curve because upper-body strength depends on a mix of body mass, leverages, and technique. The data suggests that bodyweight ranges matter much more than a single fixed “ideal” number.

title: Story
text:
The strongest story in the powerlifting data is that performance is not random. Across tens of thousands of lifters, total output changes in a clear pattern with bodyweight, and the best bodyweight bands are different for squat, bench, and deadlift. That makes this more than a static exercise list: it is a data story about how body size and strength interact in real competition.


                            
                                            





The dataset shows a clear rise in total output as bodyweight increases, especially through the middle-to-heavy weight classes.
Squat and deadlift follow stronger bodyweight scaling than bench, which suggests leverage and torso angle matter as much as body mass.
The most important story is that training recommendations should be weight-class-aware rather than based on a single “ideal” bodyweight for everyone.
Public meet results do not consistently include height, so the most reliable size signal in this data is bodyweight and weight-class band.

This project is now grounded in actual competition results and tells a much more useful story than a generic plan: the best training target depends on bodyweight, lift type, and the structure of the lifter’s body and class.
